text: The last two lessons gave you the tools — validation rules, picklists, before-save flows. This one is the worked example: a small, genuinely messy export, cleaned row by row, the way you'd actually do it before a real import.

Five rows from a lead-capture spreadsheet. At a glance it looks fine. Look closer and Acme Corp shows up twice with different casing and a trailing space, TX and Texas are the same state spelled two ways, the phone numbers use three different formats, and two emails are just blank.

Before fixing anything, name the category. TX versus Texas and the phone formatting are consistency problems. The blank emails are completeness problems. Acme Corp versus acme corp is something else entirely — a likely duplicate, which needs a human decision, not a formula.

Three spreadsheet formulas handle most of this before the file ever reaches Data Loader. TRIM and PROPER fix casing and whitespace. Nested SUBSTITUTE calls strip phone punctuation down to a consistent format. But watch the state column — TRIM and UPPER turn tx into TX and Texas into TEXAS, which are still two different strings. Formulas fix case, not content.

Here's the cleaned result. Rows one and two are now character-for-character identical — exactly what you want a duplicate rule to catch at import time, instead of creating two Account records for the same real company. The two blank emails are marked, not guessed at.

Two habits are worth keeping from this exercise. Never invent a value to fill a blank — a guessed email trades a completeness problem for an accuracy problem, and accuracy problems are harder to find later. And when cleanup produces matching rows, let a human or a duplicate rule decide what happens next, rather than silently merging them yourself.
You've now got every individual tool from this chapter. Next, we pull them into one best-practices checklist you can actually use.
